hook: Before candy, there were soul cakes at the door.
fact: Soul cakes were small spiced cakes, often marked with a cross of dried fruit or a cut in the top. Poorer neighbors went to the doors of wealthier households around All Hallows, singing and performing, and were given the cakes. Britannica notes that trick or treat is thought to have come from this British custom of letting the poor beg for soul cakes.
backbone: Asking at the door began as a way of feeding the poor.
source: Britannica, Halloween: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Halloween ; Clemson Cooperative Extension HGIC, Soul Cakes and the Origins of Trick or Treating: https://hgic.clemson.edu/soul-cakes-and-the-origins-of-trick-or-treating/
quote: Celebrants wear masks and costumes for parties and for trick or treat, a ritual thought to have derived from the British practice of allowing the poor to beg for food called 'soul cakes.'
visual: small round spiced cakes marked with a cross on a wooden board

hook: Children in Scotland were going door to door by the 1500s.
fact: By the 16th century, guising was common in Scotland and Ireland on All Hallows' Eve. Children in disguise made the rounds of their neighbors and were given treats, which were meant to ward off harmful spirits.
backbone: The costume came first, as a quiet form of protection.
source: Smithsonian Magazine, The Celtic Origins of Trick or Treating: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/celtic-origins-trick-treating-halloween-180984916/
quote: By the 16th century, 'guising' was common in Scotland and Ireland on All Hallows' Eve: Children, disguised as ghouls, made the rounds, receiving treats to ward off malign spirits.
visual: a child in a simple cloth mask at a stone cottage door at dusk

hook: Bobbing for apples was once a way to find a spouse.
fact: In the British courting game behind apple bobbing, the first to pull out a fruit was said to find love and marry first. In another custom, a young woman slept with her bobbed apple under her pillow, expecting her dreams to show her future spouse.
backbone: A party game once carried a real question about the future.
source: University of Missouri Extension, Apple bobbing: British game of sweet, sour or rotten courting: https://extension.missouri.edu/news/apple-bobbing-british-game-of-sweet-sour-or-rotten-courting
quote: In one variant, the first to retrieve some fruit would find her love and marry first.
visual: red apples floating in a wooden tub of water

hook: Mischief Night first shows up in writing at Oxford, 1790.
fact: The earliest known use of the term Mischief Night comes from Oxford in 1790. It then meant the night before May Day, when young people switched shop signs and overturned water tubs. Parts of New England now call the night before Halloween Cabbage Night, and Detroit calls it Devil's Night.
backbone: The urge to prank has simply moved around the calendar.
source: TIME, Mischief Night and Halloween: A Brief History of the Term: https://time.com/4093505/mischief-night-history/
quote: The oldest uses of the term 'Mischief Night' were in Britain, not the U.S., with the first known instance at Oxford in 1790.
visual: a crooked shop sign hanging askew on an old brick street at night

hook: A Minnesota town answered Halloween pranks with a parade.
fact: After years of soaped windows, tipped outhouses and cows loose on Main Street, civic leaders in Anoka, Minnesota, proposed a large Halloween celebration in 1920. That first year brought a parade, a bonfire at Bridge Square, and bags of popcorn, candy and peanuts for the children. The town has held it every year since, except 1942 and 1943 during World War II.
backbone: A town chose to give its restless kids something to belong to.
source: Anoka Halloween Inc., The History of Anoka Halloween: https://anokahalloween.com/history/ (details corroborated by Star Tribune coverage)
quote: In 1920, George Green and other Anoka civic leaders suggested the idea of a giant celebration.
visual: a small town main street at dusk with a bonfire glow

hook: Candy corn began in the 1880s, later sold as Chicken Feed.
fact: Candy corn was invented in the 1880s by George Renninger, who worked for the Wunderle Candy Company. In 1898 the Goelitz Confectionery Company, now Jelly Belly, bought the recipe and sold it as Chicken Feed, a nod to the country's farming roots. Each colored layer was once poured by hand into a kernel shaped mold.
backbone: A seasonal sweet began as a tribute to farm life.
source: Smithsonian Magazine, Candy Corn Hasn't Changed Since the 19th Century: https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/candy-corn-hasnt-changed-19th-century-180957107/
quote: It was invented in the 1880s by a man named George Renninger, who worked for the Wunderle Candy Company.
visual: a small glass dish of candy corn on a linen napkin

hook: Wartime Halloween ran on popcorn balls and cider.
fact: Sugar was among the first groceries rationed in the United States during World War II. Halloween hosts leaned on ration friendly recipes that newspapers printed before the holiday, from popcorn balls to donuts, cider and spiced cookies.
backbone: People kept the holiday by changing what they baked.
source: The National WWII Museum, Halloween on the Home Front: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/halloween-in-1940s-home-front
quote: When it comes to Halloween, sugar is king and that was one of the first grocery items rationed during the war years.
visual: popcorn balls wrapped in wax paper beside a jug of cider

hook: Robert Burns explained Halloween fortune telling in 16 footnotes.
fact: Robert Burns wrote his poem Halloween in 1785 and published it in 1786. He added 16 long notes explaining the customs in it, such as pulling kail stalks with eyes shut and eating an apple before a mirror by candlelight to glimpse a future spouse.
backbone: A poet wrote down the quiet rituals so they would not be lost.
source: Robert Burns Birthplace Museum blog (National Trust for Scotland), Halloween: https://burnsmuseum.wordpress.com/2018/10/24/halloween/
quote: The poem itself was written in 1785 and published in 1786 within Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect.
visual: a candle and an apple in front of an old hand mirror

hook: A French abbot gave the dead their own day.
fact: The November 2 day of prayer for all the dead is credited to Odilo, abbot of Cluny in France, who died in 1048. The date was chosen to follow All Saints' Day, and by the end of the 13th century it was observed almost everywhere in the Western church.
backbone: Remembering the dead became a shared act instead of a private grief.
quote: The institution of a day for a general intercession on November 2 is due to Odilo, abbot of Cluny (died 1048).
visual: rows of small candles glowing in a stone chapel

hook: Day of the Dead grew from Mesoamerican and Catholic roots.
fact: The Day of the Dead comes from the traditions of Indigenous peoples of Mesoamerica, including the Aztecs, Toltecs, Olmecs and Maya, who saw death as a continuation of life. It blends those rituals with All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day, which Spanish colonizers introduced.
backbone: Death is treated as a continuation, not an ending.
source: Britannica, What is the origin of the Day of the Dead?: https://www.britannica.com/question/What-is-the-origin-of-the-Day-of-the-Dead
quote: The Day of the Dead originates from the ancient traditions and beliefs of Indigenous peoples of Mesoamerica, particularly the Aztecs, Toltecs, Olmecs, and Maya, who saw death as a continuation of life.
visual: marigold petals and a lit candle on a small home altar
